\"b\" đầu từ khá giống tiếng Việt. Lỗi c: Word-initial /b/ is usually easy. The main error is losing final /b/ (job → “jop” or “jo”). Close the lips and keep a little voicing.
\"ch\" tiếng Việt mềm, không chu môi và: Often too soft, with no lip rounding and no release, and final /tʃ/ (watch, much) is often lost. Round the lips and release a short “tch”.
\"t\" tiếng Việt chạm răng và không bật: Learners often use a dental /t/ without a puff of air, or drop final /t/ (light, test). Put the tongue on the ridge, release a puff of air, and keep the final sound.
/n/ là âm mũi. Hơi qua hai bên lưỡi là /: /n/ is a nasal sound. Air going around the sides of the tongue is /l/.
/n/ là âm mũi: hơi đi ra đằng mũi (bịt m: /n/ is a nasal sound: air goes out through the nose (if you pinch your nose you can't say it). /l/ is a lateral sound: the tongue tip touches the upper ridge, air flows around the sides of the tongue, and the nose is not involved. At the end of a word (school, feel), /l/ is a “dark L”: the back of the tongue rises, giving a slight “uh-w” quality – but it must not be dropped. Consonant clusters (str-, spl-, -sts, -kts) must be said together, WITHOUT inserting a vowel “uh” between the consonants.
/n/ đứng trước /p/ (âm môi) biến thành /: /n/ before /p/ (a lip sound) becomes /m/ – assimilation of place.
/s/: đầu lưỡi gần lợi trên, môi dẹt, tiế: /s/: tongue tip near the upper ridge, lips flat, a thin hiss (see). /ʃ/: tongue pulled back slightly, lips rounded and pushed forward, a deeper “shh” (she). /tʃ/ and /dʒ/ are affricates: the air is blocked completely, then released into /ʃ/ or /ʒ/ (chair, job). /ʒ/ is like /ʃ/ but voiced, and appears almost only in the middle of words (decision, usually, measure).
/t/ nằm giữa hai phụ âm /s/ và /d/ nên t: /t/ sits between two consonants /s/ and /d/ so it usually disappears: /ˌneks ˈdɔː/.
/ʃ/ môi tròn, lưỡi lùi sau; -tion, -sion: /ʃ/ rounded lips, tongue pulled back; -tion, -sion, -cial, -tial all contain /ʃ/
/ˈsaɪəntɪsts/: số nhiều của “scientist”: /ˈsaɪəntɪsts/: the plural of “scientist” → cluster /sts/. Don't shorten it to /s/.
Bắt đầu như \"u\" chu môi rồi cong lưỡi:: Start with rounded lips as for “oo”, then curl the tongue back: “red” ≈ “(oo)red”.
Bắt đầu với miệng mở rộng ở \"a\", sau đ: Start with the mouth wide open for /a/, then raise the jaw and glide the tongue toward /ɪ/.
Bắt đầu ở /e/ rồi lướt về /ə/. Trong RP: Start at /e/ and glide toward /ə/. In modern RP the ending is very light, almost a long “e”. No r.
Bắt đầu ở /e/ rồi trượt lưỡi lên về phía: Start at /e/ and glide the tongue up toward /ɪ/. The first part is stronger and longer; the end is light.
Bắt đầu ở /ə/ (miệng thả lỏng) rồi tròn: Start at /ə/ (relaxed mouth), then gradually round the lips toward /ʊ/. British English starts from “uh”, not “o”.
Bắt đầu ở /ɪ/ rồi lướt về /ə/ ở giữa miệ: Start at /ɪ/ and glide toward /ə/ in the centre of the mouth. No r at the end.
Bắt đầu ở /ʊ/ với môi tròn nhẹ rồi thả v: Start at /ʊ/ with slightly rounded lips, then relax toward /ə/. Many younger British speakers now say these words with /ɔː/ (sure = /ʃɔː/); both are acceptable.
Chèn nguyên âm sau /s/: “sơ-port” ≈ /səˈ: A vowel inserted after /s/: “suh-port” ≈ /səˈpɔːt/ = “support”. Say /spɔːt/ in one beat.
Chữ \"p\" tiếng Việt gần như không bật h: Without the puff of air, “pen” can sound like “ben”. At the end of a word (stop, help) close the lips clearly; don't drop the sound.
Chữ cuối là “e” nhưng âm cuối của “incre: The last letter is “e”, but the final sound of “increase” is voiceless /s/, so -ed is /t/: /ɪnˈkriːst/.
Cuối từ hay bị đọc thành /s/ hoặc bỏ hẳn: At the end of words it is often replaced by /s/ or dropped (dogs, because, choose). The -s ending after voiced sounds is pronounced /z/.
Cuống lưỡi chạm ngạc mềm (như /k/), hơi: The back of the tongue touches the soft palate (as for /k/), air leaves through the nose, with voicing. In English this sound never starts a word.
Cuống lưỡi chạm ngạc mềm như /k/ nhưng r: The back of the tongue touches the soft palate as for /k/, but with voicing and a lighter release.
Cuống lưỡi nâng chạm ngạc mềm, chặn hơi: The back of the tongue rises to touch the soft palate, blocks the air, then releases it. Voiceless, with a strong puff of air at the start of a word.
Cách đọc -ed phụ thuộc vào ÂM cuối của đ: How -ed is pronounced depends on the final SOUND of the base verb (not the letter). Only when the verb ends in the sound /t/ or /d/ does -ed add an extra syllable /ɪd/. In all other cases -ed is just a consonant attached to the end: /t/ after voiceless sounds, /d/ after voiced sounds and vowels.
Câu hỏi Wh- như “What do you do?” thường: What intonation does a Wh-question like “What do you do?” usually have?
Câu hỏi Wh- trung tính thường xuống giọn: A neutral Wh-question usually falls at the end.
A Yes/No question usually rises at the end.
Câu thần chú: “Tiền Đô → /ɪd/” (t, d thê: Mantra: “T and D add a syllable → /ɪd/.” For the rest, put a hand on your throat – vibration means /d/, no vibration means /t/. Note a few special adjectives pronounced with /ɪd/: naked, wicked, learned (scholarly), aged (old).
Câu “I can swim” trong giọng Anh, “can”: In the sentence “I can swim” (British English), how is “can” pronounced?
Cả /θ/ và /ð/ đều là âm “giữa hai răng”:: Both /θ/ and /ð/ are “between the teeth” sounds: place the tongue tip lightly between the upper and lower teeth (or against the back of the upper teeth), then blow air through the narrow gap. /θ/ is voiceless – only air (think, health). /ð/ is voiced – the vocal cords vibrate (the, weather). These are fricatives that can be held on, unlike the stops /t/ and /d/.
Cặp từ nào chỉ khác nhau ở âm cuối /s/ –: Which pair differs only in the final sound /s/ – /z/?
Dễ bị đọc thành \"i\" căng của tiếng Việ: Often replaced by a tense /iː/ or lengthened. Relax the mouth muscles; the sound leans slightly toward /e/ and is cut short.
Dễ lẫn với /ɪə/ (hair – here). Với /eə/: Easily confused with /ɪə/ (hair – here). For /eə/ the jaw is more open and the sound starts with “e”, not “ee”.
Dễ với người Việt; chỉ cần nhớ khép môi: Easy for most learners; just remember to close the lips at the end of a word (time, climate) instead of dropping it or changing it to /n/.
Dễ đọc thành \"u\" căng và dài, làm \"fu: Often made into a tense, long “oo”, so “full” sounds like “fool”. Relax the lips and cut the sound short.
Dừng ở ranh giới cụm hoặc dùng “Let me t: Pausing at a group boundary or using “Let me think…”
Dừng ở ranh giới cụm ý hoặc dùng cụm câu: Pausing at a thought-group boundary or using a filler phrase keeps you sounding fluent.
Giống \"ai\" trong tiếng Việt, nhớ đọc r: Like the word “eye”; remember to say the following consonant clearly.
Giống \"i\" trong \"đi\" nhưng kéo dài n: Like “ee” in “see”, held long, as when you say “cheeese” for a photo.
Giống \"ia\" trong \"mía\" nhưng phần sa: Like a short “ee” gliding into a soft “uh”: “here” ≈ “hee-uh”.
Giống \"ng\" tiếng Việt nên dễ, nhưng ha: Often an extra /k/ or /ɡ/ is added (“sing” → “sing-g”) or it is replaced by /n/. Finish cleanly on the nasal sound.
Giống \"ph\" trong \"phở\", và ở cuối từ: At the end of a word you must still hear the airflow.
Giữa \"o\" và \"a\": nói \"o\" ngắn nhưn: Between “o” and “ah”: a short “o” said with the mouth opened wider.
Giữa câu, “of” là dạng yếu /əv/, nói nha: In mid-sentence, “of” is the weak form /əv/; when spoken fast it can be just /ə/: /ə ˈkʌp ə ˈtiː/.
Giữa “go” và “out” chèn âm nào?: Which sound is inserted between “go” and “out”?
Gần \"ao\" tiếng Việt; lỗi hay gặp là bỏ: A common error is dropping the final consonant (house → “how”, mouth → “mow”).
Gần \"h\" tiếng Việt; tránh đọc nặng thà: Don't make it too harsh, like a “kh”. Watch for silent h (hour, honest) and don't drop h where it is pronounced (hair ≠ air).
Gần \"oi\" tiếng Việt nên khá dễ; lỗi ch: Fairly easy; the main error is losing the final consonant (voice → “voy”, point → “poy”).
Gần \"ua\" trong \"mua\" nhưng phần sau: Like a short “oo” gliding into a soft “uh”: “tour” ≈ “too-uh”.
Hai môi khép kín, hơi thoát ra qua mũi,: The lips close completely, air leaves through the nose, and the vocal cords vibrate.
Hai môi khép lại, giữ hơi rồi bật mạnh r: The lips close, hold the air, then release it with a burst. No voicing. At the start of a word there is a clear puff of air (hold a sheet of paper in front of your mouth and it will move).
Hai môi khép rồi mở ra như /p/ nhưng có: The lips close and then open as for /p/, but with voicing and a weaker burst of air.
Hay bị đọc thành \"d/z\" Việt hoặc /ʃ/ k: Often replaced by /z/ or /dʒ/, or devoiced to /ʃ/ (television said with /z/ or /ʃ/ in the middle). Round the lips and keep the voice buzzing.
Hay bị đọc thành \"đ\" hoặc \"d/z\" (thi: Often replaced by /d/ or /z/ (this → “dis”, “zis”). The tongue must come between the teeth, with a continuous buzzing sound.
Hay bỏ /j/ (year → \"ia\", giống \"ear\": Often dropped (year → “ear”) or hardened to /z/ or /dʒ/. Start with a very short “ee”.
Hay bỏ /l/ cuối từ (\"school\" → \"sku\": Final /l/ is often dropped (“school” → “skoo”) or mixed up with /n/. At the end of a word, keep the tongue tip lightly touching the ridge.
Hay bỏ phần trượt, đọc thành \"e\" hoặc: Often the glide is dropped, giving a single /e/, so “late” sounds like “let”. Remember to glide up to “ee” at the end.
Hay lẫn với /s/ (she – see). Với /ʃ/ môi: Often confused with /s/ (she – see). For /ʃ/ the lips must be rounded and the tongue pulled back.
Hay lẫn với /v/ (west → \"vest\") vì răn: Often confused with /v/ (west → “vest”) because the teeth touch the lip. Keep the lips rounded and keep the teeth away.
Hay đọc ngắn như \"a\" hoặc cố uốn chữ r: Often shortened, or learners try to pronounce the r (car → “car-r”). Keep it long and drop the final r.
Hay đọc ngắn như \"o\" nên \"short\" ngh: Often shortened to a short “o”, so “short” sounds like “shot”. Round the lips more and hold the sound longer.
Hay đọc thành \"a\" (cup → \"cáp\") hoặc: Often pronounced as “ah” (cup → “cap”) or as a schwa. It is a short, open “uh” with the jaw a little more open than for a schwa.
Hay đọc thành \"e\" hoặc \"a\" thuần Việ: Often pronounced as a plain /e/ or as “ah”. Open your mouth as if to say “ah” but keep the mouth shape of /e/.
Hay đọc thành \"ia\" rõ quá hoặc thêm r: Often made into an over-clear “ee-ah” or given an extra r at the end. Just say a short /ɪ/, then relax into a light schwa.
Hay đọc thành \"o\" căng của tiếng Việt: Often replaced by a tense “o” or lengthened into /ɔː/. Keep it short and open the jaw wider.
Hay đọc thành \"r\" rung lưỡi, \"z\" (ki: Often trilled, or replaced by /z/ or /l/. Don't let the tongue touch anywhere, and round the lips slightly.
Hay đọc thành \"ua\" rõ hoặc thêm r. Chỉ: Often made into a clear “oo-ah” or given an extra r. Just say a short /ʊ/ with a light glide toward a schwa.
Hay đọc thành \"ô\" đơn (go → \"gô\"). C: Often said as a single pure “o” (go → “gaw”). It needs movement: “uh” → “oo”.
Hay đọc thành \"ơ\" ngắn hoặc cố thêm r: Often shortened to a schwa or given an r-sound (work → “wurk” with a curled tongue). Hold a long, flat “er” without bending the tongue back.
Hạ hàm xuống rõ rệt, lưỡi thấp và nằm ph: Lower the jaw clearly; tongue low and forward, lips spread. Short sound, a blend between “e” and “a”.
Hậu tố -ity → nhấn âm tiết ngay trước: e: The suffix -ity → stress the syllable right before: e-lec-TRI-ci-ty /ɪˌlekˈtrɪsəti/.
Hậu tố -tion → nhấn âm tiết ngay trước:: The suffix -tion → stress the syllable right before: pol-LU-tion /pəˈluːʃn/.
Hậu tố -y → nhấn âm thứ 3 từ cuối: /fəˈt: The suffix -y → stress the 3rd syllable from the end: /fəˈtɒɡrəfi/.
Khi cần thời gian suy nghĩ, cách nào tự: When you need time to think, what is the most natural way?
Khi liệt kê “cars, buses and bikes”, giọ: In the list “cars, buses and bikes”, where does the pitch fall?
Khi nói “bad” (khác “bat”), điều gì giúp: When you say “bad” (as opposed to “bat”), what helps listeners most?
Khi phát âm /n/, hơi đi ra đâu?: When you say /n/, where does the air go?
Khi thêm hậu tố, trọng âm có thể di chuy: When a suffix is added, the stress can move to another syllable – and the vowels change with it: a stressed syllable has a full vowel, and a syllable that loses stress is reduced to /ə/. Example: ˈPHOtograph /ˈfəʊtəɡrɑːf/ → phoˈTOgraphy /fəˈtɒɡrəfi/ → photoˈGRAphic /ˌfəʊtəˈɡræfɪk/. The first “o” changes from /əʊ/ to /ə/ and back to /əʊ/.
Khá dễ với người Việt (\"ai\"), nhưng ha: Fairly easy, but the final consonant is often forgotten: “like” becomes “lie”, “time” becomes “tie”.
Không ngắt giữa giới từ và tân ngữ (“in: Don't pause between a preposition and its object (“in / Hanoi”). The other two are reasonable thought-group boundaries.
Khẳng định, giữa câu → /kən/, và nhấn và: Affirmative, mid-sentence → /kən/, with stress on “SWIM”. Only “can't” is /kɑːnt/.
Kết thúc /n/ đầu lưỡi ở trên lợi; kết th: For /n/ the tongue tip ends up on the ridge; for /ŋ/ the tongue tip stays down.
Liệt kê: lên ở các mục chưa hết, xuống ở: In a list: rise on the items that are not the last, fall on the last item to show the list is finished.
Lưỡi cao ở phía sau nhưng thả lỏng hơn /: Tongue high at the back but more relaxed than for /uː/. Lips slightly rounded, not pushed forward. Short sound.
Lưỡi lùi sau, độ cao trung bình. Môi trò: Tongue pulled back at mid height. Lips rounded and slightly pushed forward, jaw moderately open. Keep it long, with no r-colouring.
Lưỡi nâng cao ở phía trước, đầu lưỡi chạ: Tongue raised high at the front, tip lightly touching the lower teeth. Lips spread as if smiling, jaw nearly closed. Keep the sound long and tense.
Lưỡi nâng cao, lùi sau. Môi chu tròn và: Tongue raised high and pulled back. Lips rounded and tense. Keep the sound long.
Lưỡi thấp và lùi sau, hàm mở khá rộng, m: Tongue low and back, jaw fairly wide open, lips slightly rounded. Short sound. This is typical of British English (American English usually says “ah” here).
Lưỡi đặt giữa hai hàm răng như /θ/ nhưng: Tongue between the teeth as for /θ/, but with voicing.
Lưỡi ở phía trước, độ cao trung bình. Mô: Tongue forward at mid height. Lips slightly spread, jaw moderately open. Short sound.
Lỗi chèn “ơ” vào “sport” khiến từ nghe g: If you insert “uh” into “sport”, which word does it sound like?
Lỗi phổ biến: bỏ hẳn âm cuối (“price” →: Common errors: dropping the final sound completely (“price” → “pry”), replacing /s/ with a “ch”-like sound, saying /z/ as /s/ (“rise” sounds like “rice”), and saying final /v/ as /p/ or dropping it (“live” → “lip”/“li”). The fix: practise slowly, exaggerate the ending, then link the final consonant to the vowel of the next word (“fact_is”, “price_of”) so the ending appears naturally.
Lỗi phổ biến: miền Nam/miền Bắc đều có t: Common errors: mixing up /s/ and /ʃ/ so “she” → “see”, “sort” ↔ “short”; saying /tʃ/ too softly (no release, no lip rounding); saying /dʒ/ as /z/ (“job” → “zob”); and saying /ʒ/ as /z/ or /dʒ/ (“decision” → “dezision”). The fix: practise rounding the lips for /ʃ tʃ dʒ ʒ/ – all four sounds need the lips pushed forward.
Lỗi thường gặp: bỏ -s hoàn toàn (giám kh: Common errors: dropping -s completely (listeners may think your singular/plural grammar is wrong), pronouncing every -s as /s/ (in fact /z/ is more common), or forgetting the /ɪz/ syllable (“change” and “changes” sound the same). The fix: practise /z/ separately like a buzzing bee, “zzz”, with voicing, and always count the syllables in words with /ɪz/.
Lỗi thường gặp: nói đều đều (monotone) v: Common errors: speaking in a monotone for fear of mistakes, or dropping the pitch in the middle of a sentence so the examiner thinks you have finished; or rising at the end of a statement so it sounds like a question and lacks confidence. The fix: in each IELTS answer, pick the most important word at the end of the sentence and let your pitch clearly “fall” there; for an unfinished idea, keep the pitch level or slightly rising.
Mẫu trọng âm của “pollution”?: What is the stress pattern of “pollution”?
Mẹo: -s là “tấm gương” của -ed. Âm vô th: Tip: -s is the “mirror” of -ed. Voiceless → /s/ (like /t/), voiced → /z/ (like /d/), sibilants → /ɪz/ (like /t d/ → /ɪd/). Common exceptions: “says” /sez/ and “does” /dʌz/ – the vowel changes.
Mẹo: Đếm từ cuối lên. -y/-ity: nhấn âm t: Tip: Count from the end. -y/-ity: stress the 3rd syllable from the end; -ic/-ian/-tion: stress the 2nd syllable from the end (right before the ending).
Tip: “Four lip-rounding sounds: /ʃ/ /ʒ/ /tʃ/ /dʒ/.” If your lips are flat like a smile, it is /s/ or /z/.
Mẹo: “Phụ âm đi tìm nguyên âm.” Mỗi khi: Tip: “Consonants look for vowels.” Whenever a word ends in a consonant and the next begins with a vowel, treat that consonant as the start of the next word: “an‿apple” → “a napple”.
Mẹo: “Xong thì xuống, hỏi có/không thì l: Tip: “Finished = fall, yes/no question = rise, more to come = hold.” A wider pitch range sounds more enthusiastic and natural.
Mỗi cụm ý có một “nhân” – từ được nhấn m: Each thought group has one “nucleus” – the most emphasised word, where the pitch changes.
Mỗi cụm ý thường có bao nhiêu từ được nh: How many most-emphasised words does each thought group usually have?
Mỗi từ nhiều âm tiết có một âm tiết được: Every word with several syllables has one stressed syllable: louder, longer, higher in pitch, with a clear vowel. Unstressed syllables are often reduced to /ə/ or /ɪ/. Wrong stress makes a word harder for native speakers to recognise than a wrong sound. Notation: O = stressed syllable, o = unstressed; in IPA the mark ˈ comes BEFORE the stressed syllable.
Một số vùng lẫn n/l (night – light). Cuố: Some learners mix up /n/ and /l/ (night – light). At the end of a word, /n/ is sometimes replaced by /ŋ/ (“ten” → “teng”): keep the tongue tip on the ridge.
Một số vùng phía Bắc lẫn /l/ và /n/ (“li: Some learners mix up /l/ and /n/ (“light” ↔ “night”, “low” ↔ “no”). Many learners insert a vowel into clusters (“street” → “suh-treet”, “sport” → sounds like “support”) or shorten final clusters (“tests” → “tet”). The fix: for /l/–/n/, pinch your nose to check; for clusters, start from the end of the cluster and build up: “eet → reet → treet → street”.
Một tiếng \"ơ\" thật nhẹ và nhanh, gần n: A very light, quick “uh”, with the mouth barely open.
Mouth wide open, tongue low and pulled back. Lips relaxed, not rounded. Keep the sound long. In British English the letter r after it is not pronounced.
Nguyên âm trước /ɡ/ cuối từ dài hơn trướ: The vowel before a final /ɡ/ is longer than before /k/: “bag” is longer than “back”.
Người Việt hay bỏ /s/ ở cuối từ, nhất là: Final /s/ is often dropped, especially in plurals (books → “book”) and clusters (best → “bet”). Always pronounce the final hiss.
Người Việt hay đọc /θ/ thành “th” tiếng: Learners often say /θ/ as /t/ (“think” → “tink”) or /s/ (“think” → “sink”), and /ð/ as /d/ or /z/ (“they” → “day”, “clothing” → “closing”). The fix: use a mirror – you should see the tongue tip between the teeth; hold the sound “θθθθ” for a few seconds before saying the whole word.
Người Việt hay đọc ngắn như \"i\" nên \": Often shortened to /ɪ/, so “sheep” sounds like “ship”. Make it about twice as long and keep the lips spread until the end of the sound.
Người Việt hay đọc rõ từng âm tiết theo: Learners often pronounce every syllable in full, as spelled (banana → “ba-na-na”). Stress the main syllable and reduce the others to /ə/.
Người Việt quen tách rời từng âm tiết, n: Learners often separate every syllable, saying “turn – off”, “an – apple”, even adding a glottal stop between words. The result is broken, less fluent speech. On the other hand, don't overuse “wanna/gonna” in IELTS – use natural linking (/ˈwɒntə/) instead of very casual speech. The fix: mark ‿ in model sentences, practise the links slowly, then speed up gradually.
Người Việt thường bỏ hẳn -ed (“I work th: Learners often drop -ed completely (“I work there last year”), or pronounce every -ed as /ɪd/ (“work-ed”, “stop-ed”), which adds a syllable. Another error is reading from the spelling: “increased” ends in the letter “e”, but the final sound of “increase” is voiceless /s/, so -ed is /t/. The fix: identify the final sound of the base verb, then link -ed to the next word (“developed_a plan” → /dɪˈveləptə/).
Người Việt thường ngắt ở bất cứ đâu khi: Learners often pause anywhere when they need to think of a word, insert constant “um… um…”, or the opposite: speak non-stop for fear of being judged not fluent. Both lower the score. The fix: learn ready-made chunks (In my opinion, The main reason is…) to say in one breath; when you need thinking time, pause at a thought-group boundary rather than inside a group, and use natural fillers such as “Let me think…”.
Người Việt đọc mọi từ to và rõ như nhau: Learners often say every word loudly and clearly (“I – WANT – TO – GO – TO – THE – PARK”), which sounds “robotic” and makes the key words hard for the examiner to pick out. Especially risky: a strong “can” /kæn/ may be heard as “can't”. The fix: underline the content words, say them first, then “squeeze” the weak words in between quickly while keeping the rhythm.
Người bản ngữ không nói từng từ tách rời: Native speakers do not say words separately; they “stick” them together. Three main processes: (1) Linking – a final consonant joins the vowel at the start of the next word (turn‿off); between two vowels a /j/ or /w/ is inserted (the‿/j/‿end, go‿/w/‿out), and in British English a final “r” is pronounced when the next word starts with a vowel (far‿away /fɑːr əˈweɪ/). (2) Elision – /t/ and /d/ between two consonants often disappear (next door /ˌneks ˈdɔː/). (3) Assimilation – a sound changes because of its neighbour (ten people /tem ˈpiːpl/, did you /ˈdɪdʒu/).
Người học thường “giữ nguyên” trọng âm c: Learners often keep the stress of the base word across the whole family, saying “PHOtography”, “POlitical”, “ECOnomic”. This is especially noticeable in IELTS because words like economy/economic and technology/technological come up constantly. The fix: learn word families as sets, read the whole set aloud in a row and clap on the stress.
Người nói tự nhiên chia câu thành các “c: Natural speakers divide sentences into “thought groups” – each usually 3–7 words, carrying one small idea and having one most-emphasised word. There is a very short pause between groups. Pausing in the right place helps listeners follow the structure; pausing in the wrong place (between an article and a noun, between a preposition and its object) breaks the sentence up and sounds like “searching for words”.
Ngắt nhịp theo cụm ý cho IELTS Speaking: Chunking into thought groups for IELTS Speaking
Ngữ điệu là sự lên xuống cao độ của cả c: Intonation is the rise and fall of pitch across a whole sentence, centred on the most emphasised word at the end of a thought group (called the “nucleus”). Some languages use tone on each syllable to change the meaning of words; English uses intonation across phrases to show whether information is finished or not, whether you are asking or stating, and your attitude (certain, surprised, hesitant).
Như \"a\" khi bác sĩ bảo \"há miệng ra\": Like the “ah” a doctor asks for when they say “open wide”: long and deep in the throat.
Như \"ao\" trong \"cao\", nhưng cuối âm: Like “ow” in “cow”, but round the lips toward “oo” at the end and keep the final consonant.
Như \"ng\" trong \"sáng\" nhưng không có: Like the “ng” in “sing”, with no extra burst of sound at the end.
Như \"oi\" trong \"đói\", rồi thêm phụ â: Like “oy” in “boy”, then add the final consonant very clearly.
Như \"u\" trong \"đu\", nhưng kéo dài nh: A long “oo”, like the sound of the wind: “oooo”.
Như \"v\" tiếng Việt; ở cuối từ hãy kéo: At the end of a word, hold a buzzing “vvv” like a bee.
Như \"y\" trong \"yêu\": \"yes\" ≈ \"i-é: Like the “y” in “yes”: a quick “ee” glide into the vowel.
Như \"ơ\" khi đang suy nghĩ \"ơơơ…\", ké: Like the hesitation sound “errr…” while you think, held long.
Như /tʃ/ nhưng có rung: \"jeep\" khác \": Like /tʃ/ but voiced: “jeep” differs from “cheap” by the vibration in your throat.
Like breathing on a mirror to fog it up.
Như khi ra hiệu im lặng \"suỵt!\", môi c: Like the “shh!” you make to ask for silence, with rounded lips.
Như tiếng \"ừm\" khi ăn ngon, môi khép c: Like the “mmm” of enjoying tasty food, with the lips pressed together.
Như tiếng ong \"zzz\"; \"d/gi\" miền Bắc: Like a buzzing bee, “zzz”; keep it at the end of words too.
Như tiếng tàu hỏa \"choo-choo\", môi chu: Like the train sound “choo-choo”, with rounded lips.
Nói \"e\" kéo dài rồi thả về \"ơ\": \"ca: Hold a long “eh”, then relax into “uh”: “care” ≈ “keh-uh”.
Nói \"e\" rồi hạ cằm xuống thật thấp mà: Say “e”, then drop your chin very low without changing the tongue position.
Nói \"ơu\" thật liền: \"go\" nghe như \": Glide smoothly from “uh” to “oo”: “go” is “guh-oo” said as one sound.
Nói “ờ… ờ…” giữa cụm danh từ: Saying “um… um…” in the middle of a noun phrase
Nếu đọc /ð/ thành /z/, “clothing” sẽ ngh: If you say /ð/ as /z/, which word will “clothing” sound like?
Phần “-tion” trong “education” chứa âm n: Which sound is in the “-tion” of “education”?
Qua hai bên lưỡi: Around the sides of the tongue
Qua khe răng: Through the gap between the teeth
Răng cửa trên chạm nhẹ môi dưới, thổi hơ: The upper teeth lightly touch the lower lip, and air is blown through the narrow gap. No voicing.
Răng trên chạm môi dưới như /f/ nhưng ru: The upper teeth touch the lower lip as for /f/, but with voicing.
Thè đầu lưỡi ra và thổi như xì lốp xe nh: Stick the tongue tip out and blow, like a tyre slowly leaking.
Thường bị lẫn với /æ/ (pen – pan). Với /: Often confused with /æ/ (pen – pan). For /e/ the jaw opens only moderately, not as low as for /æ/.
Thường đọc quá ngắn. Hãy giữ môi tròn đế: Often too short. Keep the lips rounded to the end of the sound, especially before a final consonant (food, choose).
Thần chú: “Danh trước – Động sau – Đuôi: Mantra: “Noun first – verb second – stress before the ending.” Two-syllable nouns stress the first syllable, verbs the second, and -tion/-ic/-ity stress the syllable right before the ending.
Thần chú: “Lè lưỡi – thổi hơi.” Nếu khôn: Mantra: “Tongue out – blow air.” If you can't hold the sound on, you are saying /t/ or /d/, not /θ/ or /ð/.
Thần chú: “Một hơi – một ý – một điểm nh: Mantra: “One breath – one idea – one emphasis.” The ideal speed is not the fastest but a steady one, with pauses in the right places.
Thần chú: “Một hơi, không ơ.” Một cụm ph: Mantra: “One breath, no uh.” A consonant cluster must fit into a single beat, with “str” as one block.
Thần chú: “Nội dung thì nhấn – chức năng: Mantra: “Content words stress – function words glide.” In British English, affirmative “can” is /kən/, while “can't” is /kɑːnt/ – a clearly different long vowel.
Thần chú: “Âm cuối là nửa nghĩa của từ.”: Mantra: “The ending is half the meaning of the word.” When you record yourself, replay and listen only to the end of each word – if you can't hear anything, neither can the examiner.
Release the lips as if gently blowing out a candle.
Tiếng Anh có nhịp dựa trên trọng âm: các: English is stress-timed: content words (nouns, main verbs, adjectives, adverbs, negatives, question words) are stressed; function words (prepositions, articles, auxiliaries, pronouns, conjunctions) are usually said quickly and lightly with the vowel /ə/ – called weak forms. The time between stressed words is roughly equal, so weak words get “squeezed”.
Tiếng Việt không có âm này nên hay thay: Often replaced by /t/ or /s/: “think” becomes “tink” or “sink”. The tongue must come out between the teeth with continuous airflow.
Tiếng Việt mỗi âm tiết đều rõ và đều nha: Learners often give every syllable equal weight, saying “e-du-ca-tion” with four equal syllables, or stress the last syllable by habit (“compuTER”, “deveLOP”). The fix: when learning a new word, always note its stress pattern (oOo…), clap hard on the stressed syllable, and reduce the other vowels to /ə/.
Trong tiếng Việt, âm cuối như “t, c, p”: Learners often stop a final “t, k, p” without releasing it, and some final sounds (/s/, /z/, /v/, /dʒ/…) are hard to produce. In English, final sounds carry meaning: “rice” differs from “rise”, “life” from “live”. Pronounce the ending fully: /t/ /k/ /p/ with a light puff of air, /s/ with a clear hiss, /z/ with voicing. One more thing: the vowel before a final voiced consonant (/b d ɡ z v/) is held slightly longer – this is the key cue listeners use to tell “bad” from “bat”.
Trong “a cup of tea”, “of” thường đọc là: In “a cup of tea”, how is “of” usually pronounced?
Trong “next door”, âm nào thường bị nuốt: In “next door”, which sound is usually dropped?
Trước phụ âm cuối hữu thanh, nguyên âm đ: Before a voiced final consonant, the vowel is lengthened. This is a very clear signal that separates “bad” from “bat”. Do not add an “uh” after the final sound.
Từ nào chứa âm /ð/ (hữu thanh)?: Which word contains the voiced /ð/ sound?
Từ nào có đuôi đọc /ɪz/?: Which word has an ending pronounced /ɪz/?
Từ nào thường ĐƯỢC NHẤN trong câu?: Which word is usually STRESSED in a sentence?

giữ luồng hơi đến hết âm, không cắt ngan: keep the airflow going to the end of the sound

phụ âm cuối “chuyển” sang từ sau: the final consonant “moves” to the next word
r cuối câm, nhưng được đọc khi từ sau bắ: final r is silent, but pronounced when the next word starts with a vowel

sau âm hữu thanh /b ɡ v z ʒ dʒ m n ŋ l/: after voiced sounds /b ɡ v z ʒ dʒ m n ŋ l/ and all vowels

Âm giữa của “decision” là?: What is the middle sound of “decision”?
Âm yếu nhất, xuất hiện ở âm tiết không n: The weakest vowel, found in unstressed syllables. Tongue, lips and jaw are all relaxed in the rest position; it is very short and light.
Âm đầu của “think” là?: What is the first sound of “think”?
Đuôi -s/-es xuất hiện ở danh từ số nhiều: The -s/-es ending appears on plural nouns, third-person singular verbs (he works) and possessives (the country's). All three follow the same rule, based on the final SOUND of the base word: add the syllable /ɪz/ after sibilant (hissing) sounds; /s/ after voiceless sounds; /z/ after voiced sounds and vowels.
Đầu lưỡi chạm lợi trên (phần gồ sau răng: The tongue tip touches the alveolar ridge (the bump behind the upper front teeth), blocks the air, then releases it. Voiceless. Strongly aspirated at the start of a word.
Đầu lưỡi chạm lợi trên như /t/ nhưng run: The tongue tip touches the alveolar ridge as for /t/, but with voicing and a lighter release.
Đầu lưỡi chạm lợi trên, hơi thoát qua mũ: The tongue tip touches the upper alveolar ridge, air leaves through the nose, and the vocal cords vibrate.
Đầu từ dễ (giống \"ph\"), nhưng cuối từ: Easy at the start of a word, but often dropped at the end: “life” becomes “lie”, “laugh” becomes “la”. Keep the upper teeth on the lip and blow air at the end.
Đầu từ như \"l\" Việt; cuối từ kết thúc: At the start of a word, a clear light l; at the end, finish with the tongue on the ridge and don't close the mouth too early.
Đặt lưỡi như /θ/ rồi \"ngân\" lên; chạm: Position the tongue as for /θ/, then add voice; touch your throat and you will feel the vibration.
Đặt tay lên cổ: phải thấy rung khi nói /: Put a hand on your throat: you should feel vibration for /b/ and none for /p/.
Đặt đầu lưỡi giữa hai hàm răng (hoặc chạ: Place the tongue tip between the teeth (or just behind the upper teeth) and blow air through the narrow gap between tongue and teeth. Voiceless.
Động từ 2 âm tiết thường nhấn âm 2: /prɪ: Two-syllable verbs usually stress the second syllable: /prɪˈzent/. The noun “gift” is /ˈpreznt/.
đọc đủ từng phụ âm trong cụm: pronounce every consonant in the cluster
Ở cuối từ người Việt hay biến /ɡ/ thành: At the end of words, /ɡ/ is often turned into /k/ or dropped (bag → “back”). Keep a short voiced sound and lengthen the preceding vowel slightly.
“Do you like reading?” – ngữ điệu cuối c: “Do you like reading?” – what is the intonation at the end?
“bathe” /beɪð/ là động từ, kết thúc bằng: “bathe” /beɪð/ is a verb and ends in /ð/. “Bath” and “path” end in /θ/.
“change” kết thúc bằng /dʒ/ là âm xuýt →: “change” ends with /dʒ/, a sibilant → /ɪz/. “Schools” is /z/, “months” is /s/.
“economic” có mẫu trọng âm nào?: What is the stress pattern of “economic”?
“go” kết thúc bằng /əʊ/ (môi tròn) nên c: “go” ends in /əʊ/ (rounded lips), so /w/ is inserted: /ɡəʊ waʊt/.
“health” /helθ/: cần cả /l/ lẫn /θ/. Bỏ: “health” /helθ/: you need both /l/ and /θ/. Dropping /l/ or changing /θ/ to /t/ are both errors.
“need” kết thúc bằng /d/ nên phải thêm â: “need” ends with /d/, so the syllable /ɪd/ is added: /ˈniːdɪd/.
“pollution” là danh từ – từ nội dung. “t: “pollution” is a noun – a content word. “The” and “and” are function words, usually weak.
“present” là ĐỘNG TỪ (trình bày) nhấn âm: Which syllable is stressed in “present” as a VERB (to give)?
“rice” /raɪs/ kết thúc bằng /s/ vô thanh: “rice” /raɪs/ ends with a voiceless /s/, “rise” /raɪz/ ends with a voiced /z/.
“stop” kết thúc bằng /p/ vô thanh nên -e: “stop” ends with voiceless /p/, so -ed is pronounced /t/: /stɒpt/.
“ten people” thường được đọc như thế nào: How is “ten people” usually pronounced in fast speech?
“think” /θɪŋk/ bắt đầu bằng /θ/ vô thanh: “think” /θɪŋk/ starts with voiceless /θ/: tongue between the teeth, just blowing air.
“watch” /wɒtʃ/ kết thúc bằng /tʃ/, “wash: “watch” /wɒtʃ/ ends in /tʃ/, “wash” /wɒʃ/ in /ʃ/. “See – she” is /s/–/ʃ/, “cheap – jeep” is /tʃ/–/dʒ/.
↗ mời người kia nói tiếp: ↗ inviting the other person to continue
Lưỡi cao ở phía trước nhưng thấp hơn và: Tongue high and forward, but a little lower and further back than for /iː/. Jaw slightly more open than for /iː/, lips relaxed (not spread as in a smile). Short, loose and crisp.
Lưỡi nằm ở giữa miệng, khá thấp. Hàm mở: Tongue in the centre of the mouth, fairly low. Jaw fairly open (more open than for /ə/), lips relaxed and natural. Short and compact.
Lưỡi nằm ở giữa miệng, độ cao trung bình: Tongue in the centre of the mouth at mid height. Lips relaxed, not rounded. Keep it long, without curling the tongue for an r.
Bắt đầu với môi tròn, lưỡi lùi sau và hà: Start with rounded lips, the tongue back and the jaw fairly open (a little more open than for /ɔː/), then relax the lips, close the jaw and move the tongue forward and up toward /ɪ/.
\"đ\" tiếng Việt là âm hút hơi vào trong: Common errors are a swallowed (implosive) /d/, turning it into /z/, or dropping final /d/ (food, good). Push the air outward with the tongue tip on the ridge and make final /d/ audible.
\"c/k\" tiếng Việt không bật hơi, gần /ɡ: Without a puff of air, /k/ can sound like /ɡ/ to English ears. Release a puff of air right after /k/ at the start of a word (a puff, not a scraping “kh” friction); at the end (book, back) close the back of the tongue clearly so the sound is not lost.
Cầm tờ giấy trước miệng: nói \"key\" thì: Hold a sheet of paper in front of your mouth: when you say “key” it should flutter from the puff of air.
Cuối từ hay bị bỏ hoặc đọc thành /f/: \": Often dropped at the end of a word or said as /f/: “five” becomes “fife”, “have” becomes “ha” or “haf”. Keep the voicing to the end of the sound.
Tiếng rắn \"sss\", gần chữ \"x\" tiếng V: Like a snake's “sss”, with the tongue tip forward, not curled back.
Đầu và mặt lưỡi đặt gần vùng ngay sau lợ: The tip and blade of the tongue sit just behind the upper alveolar ridge (further back than /s/), the body of the tongue slightly raised, lips rounded and pushed forward; blow air to make a “shh” sound. No voicing.
Nói \"suỵt\" /ʃ/ rồi thêm rung ở cổ là r: Say “shh” /ʃ/ and add vibration in your throat to get /ʒ/.
Đầu lưỡi chặn hơi ở vùng ngay sau lợi tr: The tongue tip blocks the air just behind the upper alveolar ridge (slightly further back than for /t/), then releases into /ʃ/. Lips slightly rounded, no voicing, with a puff of air.
The tongue tip blocks the air just behind the upper alveolar ridge as for /tʃ/, then releases into /ʒ/, with voicing. Lips slightly rounded.
Hay đọc thành \"gi/d\" Việt (z) hoặc \"c: Often said as /z/ or /tʃ/: “job” → “zob”, “jeep” → “cheap”. The tongue must block the air just behind the ridge first, then release.
Miệng đặt sẵn cho nguyên âm theo sau, đẩ: The mouth is already set for the following vowel; push a gentle stream of air out through the glottis (throat). No voicing, no friction at the tongue or lips.
Đầu lưỡi chạm lợi trên, hơi đi ra hai bê: The tongue tip touches the upper alveolar ridge and air flows around the sides of the tongue, with voicing. At the end of a word (feel, school) it is a “dark l”: the back of the tongue is raised and the sound is slightly like “uh-w”.
Đầu lưỡi cong nhẹ lên vùng sau lợi nhưng: The tongue tip curls up toward the area behind the ridge without touching it, lips slightly rounded, with voicing. No trilling of the tongue tip. In British English r is only pronounced before a vowel (red, very); in “car” and “water” it is not pronounced.
Môi chu tròn và hẹp như /uː/, cuống lưỡi: Lips rounded and narrow as for /uː/, back of the tongue raised toward the soft palate, with voicing, then quickly opening into the following vowel. The teeth do not touch the lip.
Thân lưỡi nâng gần ngạc cứng như /iː/, d: The body of the tongue rises near the hard palate as for /iː/, with voicing, then glides quickly into the following vowel. No friction.
Bắt đầu với miệng mở rộng ở \"a\", môi t: Open the mouth wide for “a” with relaxed, unrounded lips; then close the jaw, raise the back of the tongue and gradually round the lips toward /ʊ/.
Đầu lưỡi gần lợi trên, hai hàm răng gần: The tongue tip is close to the upper alveolar ridge and the teeth are almost together; push air through the narrow gap to make a hissing sound. Lips slightly spread, no voicing.
Vị trí như /s/ (đầu lưỡi gần lợi trên) n: Same position as /s/ (tongue tip close to the upper alveolar ridge), but with voicing, making a buzzing sound like a bee.
Khẩu hình giống /ʃ/ (môi chu, đầu lưỡi ở: Same mouth shape as /ʃ/ (lips rounded, tongue tip just behind the ridge), but with voicing. Rarely at the start of a word; common in -sion and -sure.
